newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Former Jamaica prime minister Manley laid to rest.
newsitem.headline: Former Jamaica prime minister Manley laid to rest.

text.p: Thousands of people paid their respects to former Jamaican prime minister Michael Manley on Sunday, filling the main cathedral and spilling into the streets for the funeral of the legendary Caribbean leader.

Manley's flag-draped casket was carried on the shoulders of a military honour guard, preceded by 16 officiating clergymen and followed by leading dignitaries including former Venzuelan president Carlos Andres Perez, Haitian President Rene Preval and Cuban President Fidel Castro.

Castro's arrival earlier was greeted by roars from the crowd and shouts of "Fidel, Fidel," and by a standing ovation from those inside the cathedral. The only other dignitary to receive a similar welcome was Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan.
Castro later took several minutes to chat with Manley's five children, with Preval and with Farrakhan.
Tributes were read by P.J. Patterson, Jamaica's prime minister and Manley's successor, and by Manley's cousin Hugh Shearer, whom Manley defeated in the 1972 elections.
Manley died at home on March 6, aged 72, after a long struggle with cancer.
Manley left the job of prime minister in March 1992, stepping down after a bout of pneumonia in his 40th year of involvement in Jamaican public life.
His father, Norman Manley, was a national hero who was prime minister in 1962 when Jamaica gained independence from Britain.
He led the party to an election victory in 1972 and became the first Jamaican Prime Minister without cabinet experience.
His rhetoric turned left-wing, his official clothing became tropical casual and he ordered the party's "10 Steps to Socialism" printed in Kingston's biggest daily.
By 1989, however, he returned to the business suit and tie of his youth and began courting the private sector, a strategy that paid off in 1989 when the PNP and its leader returned to power.
During a trip to the United States in May 1990, Manley received praise and pledges of help from President George Bush, who said Manley "has done a first-class job in trying to move Jamaica forward."

Schoolmate and former cabinet minister David Coore remembered the schoolboy Manley as one who would "champion the cause of those who were bullied or picked on by the bigger boys," a trait that Coore said he carried into his later political life and even onto the international stage.

Patterson recalled Manley as a cricket historian, the last living founder of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), and a leader in the international anti-apartheid struggle, the Commonwealth, and the non-aligned movement.
"Take heart that this world is a much better place because he shared his time and talent with so many," Patterson said.
